# Summary and question

This page is target on the complexity analysis and practical experiment implementation of the Bell sampling on a iqp/adaptive-iqp circuits.

# Derivation

::: {#lem-ising-Bell .callout-important icon="false"}
## (Bell sampling distribution on Ising partition function)
Consider the Hamiltonian evolution
$$
U_{\rm Ry}(t) = \exp\left[i\sum_{j<k} K_{jk}t\, Z_jZ_k + i\sum_j h_j t\, Z_j\right].
$$
and quantum state $\ket{C} = U_{\rm Ry}(t = 1) \ket{+^n}$.
The Bell sampling distribution is given by:
$$
\begin{align*}
\Pr(\mathbf z,\mathbf x) &= 2^{-3n}\left|\sum_{s\in\{\pm1\}^n}\chi_{\mathbf z}(s)F_{\mathbf x}(s)\right|^2,\; \chi_{\mathbf z}(s):=\prod_i s_i^{z_i}\\
F_{\mathbf x}(s)&:=\exp\left[i\left(\sum_{i<j:\,x_i=x_j}2K_{ij}s_is_j
+\sum_{i:x_i=0}2h_i s_i\right)\right].
\end{align*}
$$
:::

:::{.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Proof (Click to expand)
Take $t = 1$ and state $\ket{C} = U_{\rm Ry}(t) \ket{+^n}$ with 
write $U_{K,h} = e^{i\,\Phi(Z)}$ with Ising energy
$$
\Phi(s) := \sum_{i<j} K_{ij}\, s_i s_j + \sum_i h_i\, s_i,
\qquad s_i  \in \{\pm 1\},
$$
so that $|\psi_{K,h}\rangle = U_{K,h}|+\rangle^{\otimes n}$. Bell sampling on two copies of $|\psi_{K,h}\rangle$ in the standard $X^{\mathbf r_x} Z^{\mathbf r_z}$-labelled Bell basis gives [@hangleiter2024bell]
$$
\begin{align*}
\mathrm{Pr}(\mathbf r) \;&=\; 2^{-n}\,\bigl|\langle \overline{\psi_{K,h}}\,|\,Z^{\mathbf r_z} X^{\mathbf r_x}\,|\psi_{K,h}\rangle\bigr|^{2}\\
&=2^{-n}\,\Bigl|\langle+|^{\otimes n}\, U_{K,h}\,Z^{\mathbf r_z} X^{\mathbf r_x}\, U_{K,h}\,|+\rangle^{\otimes n}\Bigr|^{2}
\end{align*}
$$
Here we have used the fact that $\overline{U_{K,h}} = U_{K,h}^{\dagger}$.
Expand $|+\rangle^{\otimes n} = 2^{-n/2}\sum_y |y\rangle$ and use $U_{K,h}|y\rangle = e^{i\Phi(s(y))}|y\rangle$, together with $Z^{\mathbf r_z} X^{\mathbf r_x}|y\rangle = (-1)^{\mathbf r_z\cdot(y\oplus \mathbf r_x)}\,|y\oplus \mathbf r_x\rangle$. The two $|+\rangle$ envelopes collapse the doubled $y$-sum into a single sum. Defining $s_i(y) = (-1)^{y_i}$, we get the result:
$$
\begin{align*}
&\langle+|\, U_{K,h}\, Z^{\mathbf r_z} X^{\mathbf r_x}\, U_{K,h}\, |+\rangle
\;=\; 2^{-n}\!\sum_{y\in\{0,1\}^n} (-1)^{\mathbf r_z\cdot y}\,
e^{i\bigl[\Phi(s(y))+\Phi(s(y\oplus \mathbf r_x))\bigr]},\\
&= 2^{-n}\!\sum_{y\in\{0,1\}^n} (-1)^{\mathbf r_z\cdot y}\,
e^{i\bigl[\sum_{i<j} K_{ij}\bigl[1+(-1)^{(\mathbf r_x)_i+(\mathbf r_x)_j}\bigr]\, s_i s_j
\;+\; \sum_i h_i\bigl[1+(-1)^{(\mathbf r_x)_i}\bigr]\, s_i\bigr]},\\
&= 2^{-n}\!\sum_{y\in\{0,1\}^n} (-1)^{\mathbf r_z\cdot y}\,
e^{i\bigl[ 2\sum_{i<j:\,(\mathbf r_x)_i = (\mathbf r_x)_j}K_{ij} s_i s_j
+ 2\sum_{i:\,(\mathbf r_x)_i = 0} h_i\, s_i\bigr]},
\end{align*}
$$
where the global phase $(-1)^{\mathbf r_z\cdot \mathbf r_x}$ has been absorbed into the modulus.
Thus the probability of the Bell outcome $\mathbf{r} = (\mathbf{z}, \mathbf{x})$ is:
$$
\begin{align*}
\Pr(\mathbf z,\mathbf x) &= 2^{-3n}\left|\sum_{s\in\{\pm1\}^n}\chi_{\mathbf z}(s)F_{\mathbf x}(s)\right|^2,\; \chi_{\mathbf z}(s):=\prod_i s_i^{z_i}\\
F_{\mathbf x}(s)&:=\exp\left[i\left(\sum_{i<j:\,x_i=x_j}2K_{ij}s_is_j
+\sum_{i:x_i=0}2h_i s_i\right)\right].
\end{align*}
$$
:::

From @lem-ising-Bell, each Bell outcome's probability is still related tothe squared modulus of a **complex Ising partition function**, however, with a reframe effect by both $\mathbf{z}$ and $\mathbf{x}$:

- The $\mathbf x$ separate vertex into two sectors: $\mathcal{S}_0 = \{i: x_i = 0\}$ and $\mathcal{S}_1 = \{i: x_i = 1\}$.
- Only interactions between vertices in the same sector survive, i.e., $K_{ij}$ for $i,j \in \mathcal{S}_0$ or $i,j \in \mathcal{S}_1$.
- The $\mathbf z$ string acts as a parity tag $\prod_i s_i^{z_i}$ inside the partition sum. 


A direct consequence this reframe effect is that the marginal distribution of $\mathbf{x}$ is uniform, i.e., $\mathrm{Pr}(\mathbf x) = {2^{-n}}.$

::: {#lem-ising-gapp .callout-important icon="false"}
## (Maginal of $\mathbf x$ is uniform)
The marginal over $\mathbf x$ is approximately uniform, i.e., $\mathrm{Pr}(\mathbf x) := \sum_{\mathbf z} \mathrm{Pr}(\mathbf z,\mathbf x) = {2^{-n}}.$
:::
:::{.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Proof (Click to expand)
Note that
$$
\begin{align*}
\Pr(\mathbf x)
&=
\sum_{\mathbf z\in\{0,1\}^n}\Pr(\mathbf z,\mathbf x)\\
&=
2^{-3n}
\sum_{\mathbf z}
\left|
\sum_s \chi_{\mathbf z}(s)F_{\mathbf x}(s)
\right|^2\\
&=
2^{-3n}
\sum_{\mathbf z}
\sum_{s,t}
\chi_{\mathbf z}(s)\chi_{\mathbf z}(t)
F_{\mathbf x}(s)\overline{F_{\mathbf x}(t)} .
\end{align*}
$$
Since $\chi_{\mathbf z}(s)$ is the Fourier character on the $\{\pm\}$ field, we conclude:
$$
\sum_{\mathbf z\in\{0,1\}^n}
\chi_{\mathbf z}(s)\chi_{\mathbf z}(t)
=\sum_{\mathbf z}
\prod_i (s_i t_i)^{z_i}=\prod_i(1+s_it_i)=2^n\delta_{s,t}.
$$
Plugging back, we get:
$$
\begin{align*}
\Pr(\mathbf x)&=
2^{-3n}\sum_{s,t}2^n\delta_{s,t}
F_{\mathbf x}(s)\overline{F_{\mathbf x}(t)}\\
&=2^{-2n}
\sum_s |F_{\mathbf x}(s)|^2=
2^{-2n}\cdot 2^n=
2^{-n}.
\end{align*}
$$
Here we use the fact that $|F_{\mathbf x}(s)|=1$ is satisfied for all $s\in\{\pm1\}^n$.
:::

@lem-ising-gapp directly implies that $\mathbf{x}$ can be uniformly sampled first,
and the classical hardness must comes from the conditional distribution $\mathrm{Pr}(\mathbf{z} \mid \mathbf{x})$.

Given a fixed $\mathbf{x}$, it randomly adds color to the $n$ vertex and remove edge that connect vertices with different colors.
This will cause **percolation effect** on the Ising partition function,
if the $K_{ij}$ is somehow sparse and local.
This might make the calculation/weak simulation of $\mathrm{Pr}(\mathbf{z},\mathbf{x})$ tractable.



# Hardness proof

# Verification

::: {#thm-ising-Bell-verification .callout-important icon="false"}
Given a quantum state $\ket{C} =\exp \left[i\left(\sum_{j<k}K_{jk}tZ_jZ_k+\sum_j h_jtZ_j\right)\right] \ket{+^n}$,
There must exist a set of Pauli operators
$$
\begin{align*}
\widetilde X_i =
X_i\,
\exp\!\left[
-2it\,Z_i
\left(
h_i+\sum_{j\in N(i)}K_{ij}Z_j
\right)
\right],
\end{align*}
$$
such that $1-F(\rho,\ket{C}) \le \sum_i \frac{1-\langle \widetilde X_i\rangle_\rho}{2}$ must be hold 
:::

:::{.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Proof (Click to expand)
[t.b.c.]
:::

The check has expansion $\tilde{X}_j = \sum_{k \in \mathcal{A}_j} c_{j,k}\,\sigma (\mathbf{z}_k, \mathbf{x}_k)$, 
with $\sigma (\mathbf{z}, \mathbf{x}) = i^{\mathbf{z} \cdot \mathbf{x}} X^{\mathbf x}Z^{\mathbf{z}}$ being the sympletic representation of $n$-qubit Pauli operators. 
Given Bell measurement samples $\mathbf{r}_i := (\mathbf{r}_{i,z}, \mathbf{r}_{i,x})$,
Alice can checks
$$
[\mathrm{tr}(\sigma (\mathbf{z}_k, \mathbf{x}_k) \cdot \rho)]^2 \;=\;
\mathbb{E}_{(\mathbf{r}_{z},\mathbf{r}_{x})} (-1)^{\mathbf{r}_{z} \cdot \mathbf{x}_k + \mathbf{r}_{x} \cdot \mathbf{z}_k + \mathbf{z}_k \cdot \mathbf{x}_k}
$$
In the local IQP-case, the $\mathbf{x}_k$ being non-zero on a single position $j$ (the central vertex of $\tilde{X}_j$) and $\mathbf{z}_k$ supported on $\mathcal{A}_j$ (site adjacent to $j$) that contains at most $2^h$ indexes.
This gives an **efficient honest-prover** verification method:

:::{.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Algorithms (Bell sampling check)

1. Alice randomly sampling local IQP circuits form certain circuit ensemble $C \in \mathcal{C}$.
2. Given that $C$ is sended to Bob, he is asked to prepare $C \ket{+}^{\otimes n} \otimes C \ket{+}^{\otimes n}$ and implement the Bell measurements on this $2n$-qubits state with meausrement result $(\mathbf{z},\mathbf{x})$. This measurement result then sended to Alice.
3. Based on $C$, calculate the expansion of $\widetilde X_i$ on the Pauli basis.
4. Utilized the samples $(\mathbf{z},\mathbf{x})$, we estimates $|\mathrm{tr}(P \rho)|$. To estimate the $\widetilde{X}_j$, we try at most $2^h$ signal, where $h$ is the number of adacent edges of the vertex $j$.
5. Pass if all those average match as expected, i.e., $\langle \widetilde{X}_j \rangle_\rho = +1, \forall j$.
:::

However, the public-Pauli + squared-moment check is **not** adversarially sound on its own.
A spoof strategy eixsts:

:::{.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Algorithms (Spoof the Bell Pauli-average check)

- Based on $C$, Bob calculates the expansion coefficients $c_{j,k}$ of checks. Since $\tilde{X}_j$ is unitary with $\tilde{X}_j^2 = I$,
the squared coefficients form a probability distribution: $\sum_{k \in \mathcal{A}_j} c_{j,k}^2 = 1$.
- Bob first uniformly samples $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{F}_2^{n}$, then independently and pointwise samples each bit $z_j \in \{0,1\}$ via
$$
P(z_j = 0\mid\mathbf{x}) = \frac{1 + \sum_{k \in \mathcal{A}_j} c_{j,k}^2(-1)^{\chi(j,k)}}{2},\qquad
\chi(j,k) := \mathbf{x} \cdot \mathbf{z}_k + \mathbf{z}_k \cdot \mathbf{x}_k\pmod 2.
$$
The bracketed sum lies in $[-1,1]$ since $\sum_k c_{j,k}^2 = 1$, so the rule is a valid Bernoulli. Equivalently, $\mathbb{E}[(-1)^{z_j}\mid\mathbf{x}] = \sum_{k\in\mathcal{A}_j} c_{j,k}^2(-1)^{\chi(j,k)}$. Bob outputs the Bell transcript $\mathbf{r}_i = (\mathbf{z},\mathbf{x})$.

:::

After getting samples $\mathbf{r}_i := (\mathbf{r}_{i,z}, \mathbf{r}_{i,x})$, Alice estimates $[\mathrm{tr}(\sigma (\mathbf{z}_k, \mathbf{x}_k) \cdot \rho)]^2$ by averaging the Bell character. Using $\mathbf{r}_z\cdot\mathbf{x}_k = r_{z,j}$ (since $\mathbf{x}_k$ is supported only at the central vertex $j$ of $\tilde{X}_j$), tower expectation over $r_{z,j}\mid\mathbf{r}_x$, and Bob's spoof rule:
$$
\begin{align*}
[\mathrm{tr}(\sigma (\mathbf{z}_k, \mathbf{x}_k)\,\rho)]^2
&= \mathbb{E}_{(\mathbf{r}_{z},\mathbf{r}_{x})}(-1)^{\mathbf{r}_{z}\cdot\mathbf{x}_k + \mathbf{r}_{x}\cdot\mathbf{z}_k + \mathbf{z}_k\cdot\mathbf{x}_k}\\
&= (-1)^{\mathbf{z}_k\cdot\mathbf{x}_k}\,\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{r}_x}\!\left[(-1)^{\mathbf{r}_x\cdot\mathbf{z}_k}\,\mathbb{E}[(-1)^{r_{z,j}}\mid\mathbf{r}_x]\right]\\
&= (-1)^{\mathbf{z}_k\cdot\mathbf{x}_k}\sum_{m\in\mathcal{A}_j} c_{j,m}^2(-1)^{\mathbf{z}_m\cdot\mathbf{x}_m}\,\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{r}_x}(-1)^{\mathbf{r}_x\cdot(\mathbf{z}_k + \mathbf{z}_m)}\\
&= (-1)^{\mathbf{z}_k\cdot\mathbf{x}_k}\sum_{m\in\mathcal{A}_j} c_{j,m}^2(-1)^{\mathbf{z}_m\cdot\mathbf{x}_m}\,\delta_{\mathbf{z}_k,\mathbf{z}_m}\\
&= c_{j,k}^2.
\end{align*}
$$
The third line substitutes $\chi(j,m) = \mathbf{x}\cdot\mathbf{z}_m + \mathbf{z}_m\cdot\mathbf{x}_m$ from Bob's rule; the fourth uses Fourier orthogonality of characters on $\mathbb{F}_2^n$.

Hence, Alice's squared-moment estimator returns exactly $c_{j,k}^2$, the value she would have obtained from the honest state $\ket{C}$. The $2^h$ sign search then lifts $\sqrt{c_{j,k}^2}$ back to the signed coefficient $c_{j,k}$, so for every $i$ she reconstructs
$$
\langle \tilde{X}_i\rangle_\rho \;=\; \sum_{k\in\mathcal{A}_i} c_{i,k}\cdot\mathrm{sgn}(c_{i,k})\,|c_{i,k}| \;=\; \sum_{k\in\mathcal{A}_i} c_{i,k}^2 \;=\; 1.
$$
The witness in @thm-ising-Bell-verification collapses to $\sum_i (1 - \langle\tilde{X}_i\rangle_\rho)/2 \approx 0$, and Alice accepts with a near-unit fidelity certificate. Yet Bob's transcript is a purely classical bit-string drawn in $O(n\cdot 2^h)$ time per sample — no quantum state was prepared. The loophole is structural: every checked Pauli is publicly derivable from $C$, only its squared moment is constrained, and the sign-search step is symmetric in $\pm c_{j,k}$, so Bob can reverse-engineer a classical distribution that hits every public Fourier target.

:::{.callout-important icon="false"}
## Question
What if Alice randomly check the non-linear average of $\{\mathrm{tr}(\rho^2), [\mathrm{tr}(P \rho)]^2, \mathrm{tr}(P\rho P \rho)\}$, with symmetric linearizaiton $\mathrm{SWAP}^{\otimes n}, P \otimes P,\mathrm{SWAP}^{\otimes n} \cdot (P \otimes P)$.
:::
